label: Tehillim (Psalms) — Part 1 — Psalms 1–20
summary_plain: Tehillim opens with the two paths: the righteous who delight in YHWH's Torah, and the wicked who are like chaff. YHWH sets his anointed on Tziyon. The heavens declare the glory of The Creator. YHWH is my shepherd — I shall not want. Psalm 19 declares: the Torah of YHWH is perfect, restoring the soul. Psalm 8 asks: what is man that you are mindful of him? These are prayers, praises, and declarations spoken directly to YHWH.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads Tehillim from the Dead Sea Scrolls witnesses (11QPsa, 4QPsa-q, and additional fragments) and the Orit Ge'ez. The DSS Psalms Scroll (11QPsa) preserves a different arrangement than the Masoretic — including additional psalms (151, 154, 155) and a prose composition about David's writings. The Qumran arrangement demonstrates that the Psalter was not yet fixed in the form the Masoretes later standardized. Psalm 14 in the DSS differs from the Masoretic in significant readings.

key_terms.definition: The Psalter's opening: two ways set before every person — the way of the righteous (meditating on YHWH's Torah, like a tree planted by water) and the way of the wicked (like chaff blown away). No middle ground.
YHWH's royal psalm: the nations rage against YHWH's anointed (mashiakh) on Mount Tzion; YHWH laughs at them and declares the mashiakh YHWH's son and king.

'You are my son; today I have begotten you.' YHWH's declaration over the anointed king at his enthronement. Ancient royal covenant formula; NT writers borrowed it, applying it to the invented figure. The original is an ancient Hebrew royal enthronement text.

Opens: 'My El, my El, why have you forsaken me?' — a lament of acute abandonment followed by triumphant praise. Contains imagery borrowed wholesale by NT writers: encircling enemies like bulls and dogs, bones out of joint, divided garments by lot. The original ancient text; NT borrowing is documented here.

The best-known psalm: 'YHWH is my shepherd; I shall not want.' The shepherd imagery, the valley of deep shadow, the anointed head, the table before enemies — all covenant trust expressed through pastoral metaphor.

Hebrew imperative: 'Praise YHWH!' — a compound of hallelu (praise, pl.) and Yah (the shortened divine name). Appears throughout Tehillim especially in the closing books (Ps.146-150, the final Hallel).
Common psalm superscription: 'A psalm of/for/by David.' The Hebrew preposition lamed allows multiple meanings — dedicated to David, in David's style, or composed by David.
A term appearing 71 times in Tehillim and 3 times in Havaqquq; exact meaning uncertain but likely a musical or liturgical pause marker — either a rest in the music or a signal to lift the voice.

The header lines added to many psalms identifying the author, the occasion, the musical instrument or tune, or the liturgical use. These headers are considered part of the canonical text in the Hebrew tradition.
The complete collection of 150 (or 151 in some traditions) psalms, organized into five books, each ending with a doxology. The five books parallel the five books of Torah in structure.

faq.question: What is the significance of Psalm 1 as the opening psalm of the Psalter?
faq.answer: Psalm 1 functions as an introduction to the entire Psalter. It sets the binary framework — two ways, two destinies — that runs through the whole collection. The righteous person who meditates on YHWH's Torah is rooted like a tree; the wicked are rootless like chaff. The Psalter begins by grounding all praise, lament, and petition in the covenant relationship defined by Torah faithfulness.

faq.question: What is Psalm 2 and why is it important for understanding Hebrew covenant kingship?
faq.answer: Psalm 2 is a royal enthronement psalm celebrating the anointed (mashiakh) king on Mount Tzion as YHWH's chosen ruler. The nations' conspiracy against him fails because YHWH has established the king and declares him 'my son.' This ancient Hebrew royal covenant language — 'you are my son, today I have begotten you' — was later borrowed by NT writers for their invented figure. The original is about covenantal adoption of the Hebrew king.

faq.question: Why does Psalm 22 matter as an ancient source text?
faq.answer: Psalm 22 is a lament psalm that moves from extreme suffering to confident praise. Its specific imagery — enemies circling like bulls and dogs, bones out of joint, strength dried up like a potsherd, garments divided by lot — was borrowed by NT writers to construct their crucifixion narrative. Every detail they describe as 'fulfillment' comes directly from this ancient psalm. The direction is ancient text → NT construction, not prophecy fulfilled.

faq.question: What is the structure of Psalm 23 and what covenant relationship does it express?
faq.answer: Psalm 23 uses the pastoral metaphor of a shepherd caring for a sheep through two movements: verses 1-4 describe YHWH as shepherd (green pastures, still waters, valley of shadow, comfort with rod and staff), and verses 5-6 shift to YHWH as host preparing a feast. Together they express total covenant care — YHWH provides, protects, restores, guides, and honors the one who trusts in the divine shepherd.

faq.question: What does Selah mean in the Psalms?
faq.answer: Selah appears 71 times in Tehillim and its precise meaning is uncertain. The most likely explanations are that it marks a musical pause (a rest in the performance), a signal to lift the voice to full volume (from the Hebrew root meaning 'to lift'), or a cue for a musical interlude. It likely served a liturgical and musical function in the Temple or synagogue setting.

faq.question: What is a 'Mizmor le-David' superscription and what does it tell us?
faq.answer: Many psalm headers read 'Mizmor le-David' — a psalm of/for/by David. The Hebrew preposition lamed is flexible: it can mean dedicated to, in the style of, associated with, or composed by David. The Psalter attributes 73 psalms to David through these superscriptions. Some superscriptions also specify historical occasions (e.g., Ps.51 — 'when Nathan came to him after he had gone into Batsheva').

faq.question: What is the theological tension in Psalm 22 between abandonment and praise?
faq.answer: Psalm 22 opens with the cry of desolation — 'My El, my El, why have you forsaken me?' — and details agonizing suffering. But it pivots in verse 24: YHWH did not despise the affliction, did not hide the face, but heard when the psalmist cried. The psalm ends with universal praise — all nations, all generations, the future seed declaring YHWH's righteousness. The structure models moving through abandonment to trust through the evidence of YHWH's past faithfulness.

faq.question: How does Psalm 8 contribute to Hebrew anthropology?
faq.answer: Psalm 8 asks 'What is man that you are mindful of him?' and answers with a stunning affirmation: humanity is made slightly lower than the heavenly beings (elohim), crowned with glory and honor, given dominion over creation. This is the covenant community's self-understanding — not insignificance before the cosmos but honored stewardship given by YHWH. The psalm frames human dignity as a covenant gift, not an inherent claim.

faq.question: What makes Psalm 19 distinctive among the early psalms?
faq.answer: Psalm 19 joins two separate hymns: the first (vv.1-6) praises YHWH through creation — the heavens declare YHWH's glory without words, and the sun runs its course like a champion. The second (vv.7-14) praises YHWH through Torah — the Torah is perfect, sure, right, pure, clean, true, and more desirable than gold, sweeter than honey. Creation and Torah are paired as two witnesses to YHWH's character and instruction.

faq.question: Why does Psalm 34:8's invitation — 'taste and see that YHWH is good' — matter?
faq.answer: It moves covenant knowledge from intellectual assent to experiential encounter. The invitation is not to hear about YHWH's goodness secondhand but to taste it personally — to discover through one's own lived experience that taking refuge in YHWH is real, not theoretical. The blessing that follows — 'blessed is the man who takes refuge in him' — is a promise backed by the psalmist's own testimony of rescue.
